In addition, while it is possible for a select few to escape poverty this way or others, it is not possible for everyone. Our economic system structurally requires there to be a large pool of low income labour. There simply isn't a market for 8 billion coffee shops. So the "work hard, start a business & escape poverty" is only an *opportunity* that (in an ideal meritocracy) everyone would have equal chance of attaining, it simply cannot end poverty itself. It solves poverty for the lucky individual, it cannot end poverty itself.

62943770
The 8 hour work day is a relic from when most people performed manual labor. You can get more than 8 hours of manual labor out of people but it's not sustainable. It's why places like oil rig platforms that have 12 hour shifts give workers 2 weeks on shift, 3 weeks off, to recuperate. Without long rests between grueling work shifts the workers just burn out, irrecoverably.

Shorter shifts, with breaks during the work day, allows you to keep workers productive with less time off.

But absolutely none of this applies to people working in an office, doing knowledge work. The reality is, if you mainly work with your brain, productivity is not as simple as moving your body and performing a simple mechanical task. There are days where you are highly productive, and days where you are not, regardless of how many hours you spend in the office and allegedly "on task". In many cases, the office itself is a source of distraction and disruption to productivity, yet managers insist their direct reports be in the office so they can micro manage them and feel important.

In my own case, an average day at the office gives me maybe 2 hours of productivity. 3 hours if I come in early, so I can get some real work done before the daily meetings start. Meetings, pings from my boss on teams, and mandatory status updates and reports to various people keeps me from becoming too deeply invested in the work which I was supposedly hired to do.

I spend more time looking busy than actually doing work. My work week could be condensed to just 12 hours a week, absent all the bureaucratic horseshit I'm forced to wade through, and my productivity wouldn't change. I would still be on-target for all my deliverables.

Many people don't. That is, they aren't productive for 8 hours, not even close, nor do they try to be, instead they keep taking little breaks by chatting with coworkers, retreating to the shitter, chasing after any available distraction, that kind of thing.

Of the people who do keep it up, there are mainly 3 types:
Some people are genuine workaholics, they exist. They get off on feeling like the most irreplaceable guy in the room, which indeed they typically are, given that most people would rather shirk their own responsibilites as much as they can. But workaholics are a minority.
Some people genuinely enjoy their job. This won't be you if you're working in an office, because office work is the most boring, inane bullshit imagineable. But if you're outdoors a lot, e.g. as a park ranger, and if your tasks are varied and if you're given a certain degree of freedom on how to solve problems, then you are about as close to the way of life of your hunter gatherer ancestors as modernity will permit and it'll feel good. You evolved for that, after all, not for sitting in front of a screen 8 hours a day. But the lucky people, too, are a tiny minority
As noted by >>62945351 most people who keep it up - despite neither enjoying their particular line of work nor the notion of being productive itself - will do so because they have dependents. More broadly speaking, they do so because they are desperate and are basically getting blackmailed. "Let yourself be tortured or else your kids will starve, what's it gonna be?" As you might imagine, substance abuse among this group is exceedingly common.

And I suppose there exist some goycattle NPCs, too, who grow used to happily obeying whatever their masters ask of them, but I'm not sure I've ever met anyone like that.
